title: The Tyranny of Shipyard Cost-Plus Contracting
gist: The commander of Norfolk Naval Shipyard argues that cost-plus and level-of-effort contracting for private-sector work performed inside public shipyards is an underexamined driver of warship maintenance delays, because it pays for labor hours rather than outcomes and actively deters contractors from investing in productivity-raising automation.

themes.theme: The scale of the readiness loss

insights.claim: A recent GAO report found that over the past 10 years maintenance delays for U.S. attack submarines produced 15,000 lost operational days and an estimated $3.4 billion in costs.
insights.so_what: A quantified $3.4 billion and 15,000-day readiness hole is the budget justification for any contracting or shipyard-capacity reform package — watch for it in appropriations arguments.
insights.quote: maintenance delays for attack submarines have resulted in 15,000 lost operational days and an estimated $3.4 billion in costs
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: The Navy has contracted out half of an aircraft carrier availability and just over 30 percent of a submarine availability to private vendors at Norfolk Naval Shipyard, meaning private contracting terms govern a large share of public-yard output.
insights.so_what: Private vendors already execute a third to a half of public-yard work, so contract-structure reform is a lever over a much larger revenue pool than 'private yard' framing implies.
insights.quote: the Navy has contracted out half of an aircraft carrier availability and just over 30 percent of a submarine availability to private vendors at Norfolk Naval Shipyard
insights.locator: Because of traditionally high volumes of work
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: The well-known causes of maintenance delay — aging hulls, complex systems, workforce shortages, material delays and growing requirements — leave out contracting structure, which the author identifies as a significant and underexamined bottleneck.
insights.so_what: If the binding constraint is contractual rather than physical, reform is cheap and fast relative to building new drydocks — a different and underpriced path to fleet availability.
insights.quote: another significant and underexamined bottleneck is how the Navy contracts for private sector ship repair work performed at its public shipyards
insights.locator: This problem of maintenance delays has bedeviled the Navy for decades
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: Work placed at a private shipyard typically ends in a firm-fixed-price contract, while private-sector work performed inside public shipyards is often structured as cost-plus or level-of-effort largely for reasons of convenience.
insights.so_what: The same vendor faces opposite incentives depending on where the work sits — an arbitrage in the Navy's own contracting system that explains divergent schedule performance.
insights.quote: For a variety of reasons — largely convenience — this is not the case for private-sector work at public shipyards.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: Under a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract the contractor's effective fee percentage actually falls when costs rise, so the real problem is not excess profit but that the government absorbs nearly all downside risk from cost growth.
insights.so_what: Reframing the critique away from contractor greed toward risk allocation is what makes reform politically viable — the reform target is the risk transfer, not the margin.
insights.quote: The real problem is that, unlike under a fixed-price arrangement, the contractor generally does not bear the same degree of downside risk from cost growth: the government bears most of it.
insights.locator: The Perverse Math of the Fee
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: On a $10 million estimated-cost contract with a $700,000 fixed fee, efficient completion at $8 million raises the effective fee to 8.75 percent while cost growth to $15 million cuts it to roughly 4.7 percent — yet the contractor still remains financially whole because the government pays the extra $5 million.
insights.so_what: The worked arithmetic shows why fee-percentage arguments miss the point; the transferable lesson is that fee structure without downside exposure does not discipline cost.
insights.quote: The contractor remains financially whole because the Navy is effectively footing the bill to “keep the lights on.”
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: Cost-plus is the right tool for genuine uncertainty early in an availability, but the Navy's error is letting a mechanism designed to manage early uncertainty become the vehicle for executing the remaining work after that uncertainty has already been resolved.
insights.so_what: The prescription is temporal, not categorical: pay for uncertainty only while it exists. Any reform that bans cost-plus outright will misfire.
insights.quote: the Navy should pay for uncertainty only while uncertainty exists — and stop paying for it once that uncertainty has been resolved
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: When growth work is discovered in the drydock, the administratively easiest path is to add funding to an existing level-of-effort structure rather than scope and definitize the new requirement, which over time creates what the author calls a black hole of accountability.
insights.so_what: This is the specific mechanism by which availabilities extend indefinitely; watch whether reform targets this 'easy button' rather than headline contract types.
insights.quote: Over time, this creates a black hole of accountability.
insights.locator: The real trap springs when growth work is discovered in the drydock.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: The objection that definitizing work has itself slowed availabilities confuses contracting discipline with government process inefficiency; the fix is empowering contracting officers to decide without elevating every change, not loosening the contracts.
insights.so_what: Diagnosing the delay as internal approval latency rather than contract rigor redirects reform toward delegation authority — a cheaper and faster intervention.
insights.quote: But that objection confuses contracting discipline with government process inefficiency.
insights.locator: Critics may argue that this kind of rigor
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: When work is definitized to a measurable outcome — such as replacing a specific set of propulsion gears at a negotiated fixed price — the contractor's profit is decoupled from labor hours consumed, which is the core behavioral change the Navy needs.
insights.so_what: Outcome-based task orders are the operative reform unit; look for hull preservation and combat-system upgrades as the first competed fixed-price packages.
insights.locator: Definitized Work vs. Level of Effort
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: Under a labor-driven reimbursement model a contractor that could spend $1 million on robotic welding or digital work instructions to cut $2 million of labor would be destroying its own revenue base, so it rationally declines the investment.
insights.so_what: This is the direct mechanism by which contract structure suppresses shipyard automation capex — the key variable for anyone modeling ship-repair productivity or industrial automation demand.
insights.quote: the technology reduces the very labor hours from which revenue is generated
insights.locator: Consider a contractor that could invest $1 million in robotic welding
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: The disincentive to automate holds regardless of how much competition exists among contractors, meaning the Navy's decade-long push to increase competition in ship repair cannot by itself produce efficiency.
insights.so_what: Competition policy is the wrong lever here; efficiency gains require changing the payment basis, which reframes how to judge Navy ship-repair reform announcements.
insights.quote: That dynamic holds true regardless of how much competition exists among contractors.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: Simply adding more labor to an inefficient production model will not solve the Navy's ship-repair capacity problem; the requirement is increased throughput per worker, per dock and per dollar.
insights.so_what: Capacity expansion framed as hiring is a false solution — watch for throughput metrics, not headcount, as the real test of shipyard programs.
insights.quote: If the Navy needs to push more ships through their yard periods, it should increase throughput per worker, per dock, and per dollar.
insights.locator: This is critical as the Navy attempts to expand repair capacity.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: The Navy's contracting model determines what the private ship-repair industrial base invests in, how it organizes its workforce and how aggressively it pursues productivity — making contracting a form of industrial policy rather than an administrative function.
insights.so_what: Treat contract-type policy as the leading indicator for shipyard capital spending and automation vendor demand over multi-year horizons.
insights.quote: It helps drive efficiency by determining what the private ship-repair industrial base chooses to invest in
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

themes.theme: Thin markets and the limits of fixed-price

insights.claim: In thin markets such as submarine combat systems work, pushing maximum performance risk onto a single qualified contractor through firm-fixed-price contracts produces defensive risk premiums or no bids at all, potentially accelerating vendor exit from the defense industrial base.
insights.so_what: A caution against blanket fixed-price mandates: in sole-source niches the policy actively shrinks supply, which is a risk for specialized defense suppliers.
insights.quote: Without competitive pressure to sharpen their pencils, vendors will either price in large defensive risk premiums to protect themselves or decline to bid altogether
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: For sole-source work the Navy should use fixed-price incentive (firm target) structures with a realistic target cost, target profit and shared overruns and underruns up to a negotiated ceiling, so both parties are invested in driving down labor hours.
insights.so_what: FPIF share-lines are the specific instrument to watch in future Navy solicitations; they change margin distributions for specialized repair vendors.
insights.quote: In a sole-source scenario, the contract should function as a structured partnership.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: Multiple-award indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contracts have already reduced the single-source problem in most ship-repair areas, leaving specialized niches as the remaining exception.
insights.so_what: The competitive base is broader than commonly assumed, so fixed-price task orders are feasible for most of the work — a tailwind for outcome-based reform.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: Public and private shipyards sit at the nexus of risk transfer between the Navy's technical community, which delivers late-breaking ship change documents after planning windows close, and the operational community, which demands ever-shorter availabilities.
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on reform is upstream requirement churn plus schedule compression, so contracting reform without fixing those two inputs will fail.
insights.quote: Both public and private shipyards lie squarely at the nexus of risk transfer between the Navy’s technical and operational communities.
insights.locator: The Nexus of Risk — Why Change Is Hard
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: When late technical changes collide with compressed operational schedules, contracting officers choose the cost-plus or level-of-effort structure as an administrative survival mechanism rather than delay the start of the availability to definitize properly.
insights.so_what: The behavior is rational under the constraints, which means exhortation will not change it — only schedule slack or delegated authority will.
insights.quote: It is the administrative survival mechanism for a workforce trapped between demands for technical precision and operational speed.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: Transitioning risk to contractors will raise initial bid prices because vendors price execution risk in, and pushing too much downside too quickly onto a fragile ship-repair industrial base could drive smaller specialized vendors out of the defense market entirely.
insights.so_what: Expect headline cost increases as the first visible effect of reform — a political vulnerability that could kill the policy before productivity gains appear.
insights.quote: when contractors are asked to absorb execution risk, they will price that risk into their proposals, resulting in higher initial bids
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: Fixed-price models create their own behavioral risks: quality corner-cutting when margin is threatened, and an adversarial claim-driven environment of requests for equitable adjustment if the Navy fix-prices work that is poorly definitized.
insights.so_what: Fixed-price is not free — it shifts cost from schedule overrun into oversight and claims litigation, which should be modeled rather than ignored.
insights.quote: Instead of repairing ships, Navy project teams and vendors will spend their time fighting over technical interpretations and requests for equitable adjustment.
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh

insights.claim: In ship maintenance all parties associated with an availability should treat time as an independent variable, a discipline the author presents as the organizing principle for both contracting and internal decision-making.
insights.so_what: A testable standard for judging any Navy maintenance initiative: does it hold schedule fixed and flex scope, or does it flex schedule?
insights.quote: In ship maintenance, all parties associated with an availability should treat time as an independent variable.
insights.locator: Critics may argue that this kind of rigor
insights.speaker: Kavon Hakimzadeh
